what_it_does: Integer Linear Programming (ILP) is a mathematical technique widely used to find the best possible plan among a huge number of options — think of routing trucks, scheduling factories, or managing power grids — where the variables must be whole numbers. Solving these problems is notoriously slow: it can take tens of hours even on large computers, yet many real applications need answers in seconds or minutes. The core algorithm (called branch-and-bound, which systematically narrows down the space of possible solutions like a game of 20 questions) mostly involves multiplying together large matrices where most entries are zero (called sparse matrices — ones with lots of empty cells). SPARK reconfigures the small fast cache memory (a chip-level store sitting right next to the processor) that already exists inside a standard CPU to also act as a miniature math engine. By placing logic that detects and skips zero entries right next to where the data lives, memory movement is dramatically reduced and the repeated sparse multiplications at the heart of the ILP algorithm speed up significantly — adding only about 1.4% more chip area.
